Lucia, tell me about a project you inherited that was already in trouble when you arrived.
In 2021 I inherited a payments platform. By the time I took over, the team had lost three engineers, and the backlog had grown to eight months of work.
And what was the state of the system itself?
Bad. The platform had been unstable since 2019. Downtime was six hours a month, and nobody had ever looked for the root cause.
So where did you start?
With the cause, not the symptoms. Once we had found it, we rewrote one service and cut downtime to twenty minutes a month.
Was there a setback along the way?

One big one. In month three we lost a release, because we had not built a contingency for the data migration. After that, nothing shipped without one, and by month six the team had regained its momentum and turned the platform around.

Hi, this is the post-incident summary for last Thursday, recorded before the written report goes out. Here is what we know. The service went down at six forty in the morning. By the time the on-call engineer opened the dashboard, the queue had already grown to four hundred thousand messages, and two regions had failed over. The team restored service in fifty minutes, and that part is good. What is not good is what we found afterwards. The root cause was a configuration change that somebody had pushed on Friday evening without a review, and nobody had documented it. So the four hours we spent looking for the problem were spent in the wrong place. From now on, two rules. No configuration change ships without a review, and every change gets a contingency. I will send the full report tomorrow.

When I coach people for senior interviews, I always ask the same question first: what had already happened before you arrived? Most candidates skip that part. They start with what they did, and the interviewer has no idea whether the work was hard or easy. If you say I cut downtime to twenty minutes, that means nothing on its own. But if you say the platform had been unstable for a year, the backlog had grown to eight months, and three engineers had left before you took over, then the same sentence is a turnaround. So build every story in two layers. The earlier layer is the situation you inherited. The later layer is what you did about it. English gives you a tense for exactly that, and the candidates who use it well sound like people who understand cause, not just effort.
